q: A 28-year-old with a Fontan circulation needs a laparoscopic appendicectomy. Which feature of the circulation matters most for ventilation?
o: Pulmonary blood flow is pumped by a single ventricle
Pulmonary blood flow is passive, so raised intrathoracic pressure reduces it
The pulmonary vascular resistance is irrelevant
why: In a Fontan, systemic venous blood flows passively to the lungs. Positive pressure, high PEEP and pneumoperitoneum reduce pulmonary blood flow; keep intrathoracic pressure low and stay well filled.

q: A patient with Eisenmenger syndrome needs GA. Which change at induction is most dangerous?
o: A fall in heart rate to 70
why: With a fixed high PVR, a fall in SVR increases right-to-left shunting and causes profound desaturation. Maintain SVR and avoid rises in PVR.

q: Why are air filters placed on IV lines in adults with intracardiac shunts?
why: Air entering the venous side can cross a shunt to the systemic circulation (paradoxical embolism), causing stroke or coronary embolism.

q: A 35-year-old had a Mustard (atrial switch) operation for transposition. What is the main long-term concern?
o: Failure of the systemic right ventricle
why: After atrial switch (Mustard or Senning) the RV is the systemic ventricle and tends to fail over time. Congenitally corrected TGA has the same problem.

q: In cyanotic congenital heart disease, which induction approach helps avoid increasing right-to-left shunting?
why: Ketamine maintains SVR, so combined with etomidate, midazolam or propofol it limits a fall in SVR and the resulting increase in right-to-left shunt.

q: Which adult congenital lesion is classed as severe complexity, needing specialist-centre care?
why: Severe complexity includes cyanotic disease, single ventricle, corrected TGA, Ebstein’s and double outlet ventricle. Simple lesions can be managed in a non-specialist centre.

q: For a woman with pulmonary hypertension and congenital heart disease who becomes pregnant, what is the approximate maternal mortality?
why: Pulmonary hypertension carries a classically quoted maternal mortality of 30–50% (older series; more recent figures are lower but still high); it is mWHO class IV and pregnancy is not recommended.

q: A cyanotic adult with a haematocrit of 0.65 is listed for surgery. What does the 2026 ESC consensus advise about pre-operative phlebotomy?
o: Venesect to a target haematocrit of 0.45
Prophylactic phlebotomy to a target haematocrit is not advised
Give iron to increase the haematocrit further
why: Prophylactic phlebotomy to a target haematocrit is not advised. Secondary erythrocytosis is compensatory.

q: Why should high-risk adult congenital heart disease patients be placed first on the operating list?
o: To allow a longer post-op recovery stay
To limit dehydration from fasting in preload-dependent circulations and ensure expert staff
Because their surgery is always the longest
To reduce the risk of infection
why: Being first limits fasting-related dehydration in preload-dependent circulations (such as Fontan) and makes sure experienced staff are available.

q: A patient with a large unrepaired VSD (left-to-right shunt) is anaesthetised. Which change will increase the shunt?
why: A fall in PVR (hyperoxia, hypocarbia, alkalosis) or a rise in SVR increases left-to-right flow and can cause pulmonary over-circulation.
